new_statements.translation: 1.2.3 Suprasegmental — nasality [ँ]; accent (svarāghāt): neutral –, rising – / (this sign is used after the syllable). [p. 2] … (23) Accent — / (in the examples below the neutral accent has been left unmarked): pīr 'saint' / pī/r 'wife's natal home'; gorī 'fair-skinned woman' / go/rī 'cowherd'; paur 'last year' / pau/r 'watch of the day' [p. 6] … For the suprasegmental phoneme 'neutral accent' there is no sign in the script, which is reasonable. The rising accent is indicated by the sign ( ) placed with the syllable on which this accent is located … very often the rising accent is also left unmarked in written Modern Rajasthani. [p. 7]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bahl treats accent (svarāghāt) as a suprasegmental phoneme with two values: an unmarked 'neutral' accent and a lexically contrastive 'rising' accent attached to a specific syllable; the rising accent distinguishes word pairs that are segmentally identical (historically the syllable before a lost /h/: pīhar > pī/r, sasur > so/rī, gvālā > go/rī, prahar > pau/r, syāhī > sa/ī). He gives no rule for where the neutral accent (default word stress) falls, and no statement that stress is predictable; the description is of a lexical pitch/rising accent, not of stress placement.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; only that the rising accent is frequently left unwritten in written Modern Rajasthani.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms: minimal pairs of isolated words (pp. 6-7). Variety: standard Marwari of Jodhpur/Bikaner, phonology based on the Mathaniya and Rotunda dialects (preface p. ii). Read from the scan images (no text; my Hindi scanned checked against the page scan); the term svarāghāt is the standard Hindi term for accent/stress, and 'ārohī' (rising) marks it as a pitch contour — the same phenomenon Gusain calls 'tones' and Allen 1957 'aspiration/murmur'.
new_statements.identity_note: Bahl 1980 describes 'Modern Rajasthani' = the standard form current in Jodhpur and Bikaner (Marwari proper); the phonology chapter is based on the Mathaniya and 'Rotunda' dialects of Jodhpur district and, per the preface, applies to the other Jodhpur/Bikaner forms. This is marw1260 (Standard Marwari), the same variety Mukherjee 2011 (Jodhpur informants) describes. Note the statement is about a lexically contrastive rising accent (the well-known Rajasthani 'tone' from lost /h/), not a default word-stress placement rule.

new_statements.quote: Another interesting problem in the analysis of the Mārwāṛī vowels is that of pitch or tone. Asopa [1896:27-28] noticed that in some words, the vowels received a special 'acute' accent (udātt). [...] Bahl [1972, 1980] does describe this 'pitch' (svarāghāt) and treats it as another suprasegmental phoneme. I found that this accent is phonetically a high-falling tone, and it may occur on any vowel. [...] this tone is particularly significant in the verbal system, where, placed on the last vowel of the verb stem, it forms the "inferred future" tense. As will be shown later, this tone seems to result from loss of an [h] in the following syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Same text as index 1: confirms the catalog's 'tonal' kind (Bahl 1980 svaraghat) with independent field data; adds phonetic contour (high-falling; Bahl's label is arohi 'rising'), distribution (any vowel), diachronic source (loss of following [h] < /s/) and the grammatical inferred-future tone on the stem-final syllable; no word-stress placement statement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-stress placement rule is given anywhere in the dissertation (1.2 'Marwari Phonology', pp. 23-39, is an avowedly informal overview: 'my analysis.. did not include any attempt at true phonological investigation', p. 23; the phrase 'after a stressed vowel' is used incidentally on pp. 30 and 38 without saying where stress falls). What Magier does state is a phonemic suprasegmental TONE: Bahl's svaraghat is 'phonetically a high-falling tone' that 'may occur on any vowel', marked with an apostrophe over the vowel; it lengthens short vowels phonetically; it is phonemic with minimal pairs (p. 38, citing Asopa 1896:28-9, Bahl 1972:16, 1980:6); diachronically it arises from loss of [h] (itself often < /s/) in the following syllable, falling 'on the vowel in the syllable immediately preceding the elided consonant' (p. 38); grammatically, a high-falling tone on the last syllable of the verb stem plus -ī forms the 'inferred future' (3.2.1.9, pp. 128-129, 131: 'the regular spoken form of the inferred future is with the falling tone'). He marks the tone only where clearly distinctive.
new_statements.exceptions: Tone 'does not always arise when /s/ or /h/ are elided. (Thus [lāpī], not *[lā'pī] for /lāpsī/)' (p. 38); Magier marks the tone 'only where it is clearly distinctive, as in the case of its use as a grammatical marker of the inferred future tense' (p. 38); the phonemic status of the tone is called 'somewhat problematic' (p. 129).
new_statements.identity_note: Magier describes the spoken Marwari of Jodhpur city and district (fieldwork in Jodhpur and the village of Borunda, Rupayan Sansthan; informant/assistant Manohar Lalas), western Rajasthan; he notes sub-dialect variation (e.g. Pushkarna Brahmin speech of Jodhpur) and contrasts his data with Bahl's Marwar Mathania informant.

sources.note: Ch. 1 §1.2.3 (p. 2) lists suprasegmental phonemes: nasality, and svarāghāt (accent) with two values, nirapekṣ 'neutral' (unmarked) vs ārohī 'rising' (marked after the syllable); (23) p. 6 gives minimal pairs for the rising accent (pīr 'saint' vs pī/r 'wife's natal home', gorī vs go/rī 'cowherd', paur vs pau/r 'watch of the day'); p. 7: neutral accent has no written sign, rising accent is marked on the syllable that bears it and is often left unwritten. No rule for where the neutral accent falls; no stress-placement rule.

tone.quote: शब्दों को संक्षिप्त करने एवं अक्षर को लुप्त करने की प्रवृत्ति राजस्थानी में है । ऐसे स्थलों पर सम्बन्धकारक चिन्ह (27०57०९०7०) का: भी प्रयोग किया जाता है। अधिकतर स, ष, दा, ह आदि अक्षरों का ही इस प्रकार लोप होता है। … इन अक्षरों की विलुप्तावस्था में (/) चिन्ह अत्यन्त आवश्यक है । इसके अभाव में अर्थभेद के कारण असंगति उत्पन्न हो जाती है | दोनों के अरथभेद के उदाहरणों से यह बात अच्छी तरह स्पप्ट हो जायगी, यथा- १ चा “इच्छा चा ८ चाय २ चेरो- चेहरा चेरों - दास, सेवक नार> नाहर, सिह, दाध सार सारी, स्त्री
tone.translation: Rajasthani has a tendency to shorten words and drop letters. In such places the relational sign (apostrophe) is also used. Mostly it is the letters s, ṣ, ś, h etc. that are dropped this way. … When these letters have been dropped the (') sign is absolutely necessary. Without it, inconsistency arises through difference of meaning. Examples of the two meanings will make this clear, e.g. 1 cā 'wish' / cā < cāy 'tea'; 2 cero < cehrā 'face' / cero 'slave, servant'; nār < nāhar 'lion, tiger' / sār … sārī 'woman' [the scanned omits the apostrophe on the marked member of each pair].
tone.summary: No tone system stated: notes only that an apostrophe must be written where s/ṣ/ś/h has dropped because word pairs otherwise clash in meaning, and that 'accent' with high pitch opens close vowels.
tone.says: No tone system stated: notes only that an apostrophe must be written where s/ṣ/ś/h has dropped because word pairs otherwise clash in meaning, and that 'accent' with high pitch opens close vowels.

tone.quote: (२) डिंगल मे वहुत से शब्द ऐसे हैं जिनका उच्चारण करते समय किसी अक्षर विशेष पर जोर देना पडता है। जोर देकर न पढने से उस शब्द का अर्थ कुछ और निकलता है और जोर देकर पढने से कुछ और हो जाता है। उदाहरणार्थ मौर' शब्द को लीजिए | इसमे मौ' पर जोर देकर न पढने से इसका अर्थ पीठ होता है, १९ जोर वेकर पढने से मुहर हो जाता है। इस तरह के कुछ भौर शब्द देखिये --- … नार स्त्री नार सिह / कद उँचाई कद कंबे / नाथ स्वामी नाथ नथवधन / पीर पीडा पीर ; पीहर
tone.locator: p. 42, ch. 1 (प्रथम प्रकरण) > 'डिंगल भाषा का संक्षिप्त व्याकरण' > उच्चारण item (२)
tone.translation: (2) In Dingal there are many words in pronouncing which one must put force [jor, emphasis] on a particular syllable. Read without the force the word yields one meaning, and read with the force it becomes another. For example take the word 'maur': read without force on 'mau' it means 'back', and read with force it becomes 'seal/gold coin (muhar)'. See some more words of this kind --- ... nar 'woman' / nar 'lion'; kad 'height' / kad 'when' [scanned-garbled gloss]; nath 'master' / nath 'nose-ring'; pir 'pain' / pir 'wife's natal home (pihar)'.

tone.quote: राजस्थानी श्रादि इन सब भाषाओं में Phonetics या उच्चारण-तत्व से झमिज्ञ गवेषक के द्वारा इस विषय पर खोज होनी 'चाहिये। जहां ae मुझे ज्ञात EMT, इस विषय के सम्बन्ध में राजस्थानी के लिये ऐसे कुछ सूत्र किये जा सकते हैं-- … (2?) घोष महाप्राण, “ घ के ढ थ भ ”, शब्द के आदि में रहने से; वे कणट-नालीय स्पर्श से सिल्ित हो जाते हैं । … (३) घोष मदाप्राण, शब्द के मध्य अथवा अन्त में रहने से, उनका असर शब्द के श्राद्य अक्षर पर पढ़ता है- … arr अक्षर के say से ae कथठ-नालीय स्पृष्ट ध्वनि az जाती है ।

tone.translation: In all these languages, Rajasthani etc., this matter should be investigated by a researcher versed in Phonetics. As far as I have learnt, for Rajasthani some such rules can be framed on this matter-- ... (2) the voiced aspirates 'gh jh(?) dh dh bh', when word-initial, become mixed with a glottal contact. ... (3) voiced aspirates, when word-medial or final, have their effect on the initial syllable of the word- ... a glottal-constricted sound comes onto the initial syllable.

tone.quote: (b) SMe. [hati] ‘companion’, beside [fati] ‘ elephant’. In view of the restriction which excludes aspirates from non-initial position in this dialect (see (ii) (b) above), no non-initial [h] is found < *s: instead one finds a lengthening of the preceding vowel together with a rising pitch-pattern—thus [haaro] | mother-in-law’s house’ (also [ha’*ro], [ha"?ro]), beside [haro] ‘ brother-in-law’ (cf. H. salo). A similar phenomenon is found more generally in Me. in future tense forms (presumably from *-s-) …
